Nigeria’s cryptocurrency economy contracted by three per cent to $38.1bn or N51.44tn in the year to June 2026, despite remaining one of the largest digital asset markets in Sub-Saharan Africa, as activity on decentralised exchanges and cross-border peer-to-peer platforms declined. The decline came amid efforts by Nigerian regulators to strengthen oversight of the cryptocurrency industry, with the Securities and Exchange Commission introducing tighter requirements for digital asset operators and the Central Bank of Nigeria moving to establish a licensing framework for stablecoins and other virtual assets. According to the 2026 Geography of Cryptocurrency Report by blockchain analytics firm, Chainalysis, Nigeria’s cryptocurrency activity fell from its previous level, with a 45 per cent decline in decentralised exchange transactions and a 17 per cent drop in cross-border peer-to-peer flows outweighing growth in centralised exchanges and other cryptocurrency services. The report measured cryptocurrency value received between 1 July, 2025 and 30 June, 2026. Nigeria ranked third globally in grassroots cryptocurrency adoption, indicating that digital assets continued to attract substantial participation from individuals and businesses despite the contraction in transaction activity. Nigeria’s performance contrasted with that of South Africa, whose cryptocurrency economy expanded by 52 per cent to $39.3bn during the period. Together, the two countries accounted for more than three-quarters of cryptocurrency activity in Sub-Saharan Africa, where the market grew by 13.4 per cent to $101bn, making it the fastest-growing region globally. In August 2026, the SEC admitted three additional virtual asset service providers, including Yellow Card Financial, Pisi Payments Solution and BC Access, into its Accelerated Regulatory Incubation Programme. The initiative allows eligible players to operate within specified conditions while the commission assesses their business models and compliance with regulatory requirements. The commission subsequently proposed new rules covering digital asset exchanges, custodians, stablecoins, peer-to-peer trading and tokenisation platforms. The proposals include higher capital requirements and registration obligations for operators seeking to provide digital asset services in Nigeria. In a further development, the Central Bank of Nigeria issued its regulations for the Operations of Non-Security Virtual Assets in Nigeria on 5 November, 2026. The framework provides for the licensing and supervision of stablecoin issuers and virtual asset service providers involved in payments, transfers, custody, remittances and settlement. The developments followed President Bola Tinubu’s July 2026 Executive Order on Virtual Assets Coordination, which established a council chaired by the CBN, with the SEC and Nigeria Revenue Service as vice-chairs, to improve coordination among government agencies responsible for the sector. Amid these regulatory changes, the Chainalysis report identified practical financial needs as a major driver of cryptocurrency adoption across Sub-Saharan Africa, particularly demand for cheaper cross-border payments, access to dollar-denominated value and alternative ways of managing personal finances. For businesses, digital assets provide another channel for settling international transactions and moving money across markets, particularly where conventional payment systems are expensive or inefficient. Stablecoin and Blockchain Commercial Lead at Nigerian fintech company Flutterwave, Mercy Emmanuel, said the commercial value of blockchain technology in African markets would depend on its ability to address existing financial challenges. “For African markets, the most commercially relevant innovations will be those that reduce friction in existing financial activities rather than those that introduce complexity simply for the sake of using blockchain technology,” she said. The report identified stablecoins, personal wallets and business-orientated transactions as important components of cryptocurrency adoption in the region, reflecting demand for greater control over funds, dollar-linked value and practical payment solutions. South Africa’s growth was broad-based, with increases across every transaction category measured by Chainalysis. Cross-border peer-to-peer stablecoin flows and service-related transactions were among the leading contributors. Nigeria, however, recorded a different pattern, as the decline in decentralised exchange activity and cross-border peer-to-peer flows outweighed gains in centralised exchange and other cryptocurrency services.
